461.quote_or_event: “Do not do any evil at all; look ahead to the future with foresight. So throw the dice in such a way, that you shall not lose with your Lord and Master. Do those deeds which shall bring you profit.”
461.explanation: In a pauri of Asa Ki Vaar, Guru Nanak tells the seeker to look far ahead before acting, to play life's game so as not to lose, and to do only what yields profit.
461.tie_back: The Kural asks for a reckoning of cost, gain and final yield before acting; Guru Nanak likewise asks for long foresight and deeds chosen for their profit.
461.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
461._accuracy_note: A strong fit on foresight and acting for profit; Gurbani's profit is standing before God, not the worldly balance sheet the Kural has in mind.

462.quote_or_event: “The chosen ones, the self-elect, are accepted and approved. The chosen ones are honored in the Court of the Lord. … The chosen ones meditate single-mindedly on the Guru.”
462.explanation: In the sixteenth pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak praises the panch, the chosen ones whose minds are fixed on the Guru, as accepted and pre-eminent. Later Sikh tradition took the five chosen Sikhs as the model for weighty collective decisions.
462.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is hard for those who deliberate with a well-chosen circle; Japji Sahib honours just such a tested, chosen company.
462.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
462._accuracy_note: Partial: the verse praises the chosen ones but does not speak of taking counsel with them; the link to collective deliberation comes from later Sikh practice, not this text.

463.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukhs lose their capital, and still, they demand profits. How can they earn any profit?”
463.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the trader's language of capital and profit: the self-willed squander their principal and still expect a return.
463.tie_back: The Kural warns against losing one's capital in the hope of future profit; Guru Amar Das calls it folly to lose the capital and still expect a gain.
463.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1131, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
463._accuracy_note: Strong on the capital-and-profit ledger; in Gurbani the capital is spiritual (the Name, the human life), and the warning is against squandering it rather than against risky ventures.

464.quote_or_event: “Fareed, those deeds which do not bring merit - forget about those deeds. Otherwise, you shall be put to shame, in the Court of the Lord.”
464.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker to drop any undertaking that brings no merit, lest it end in shame.
464.tie_back: The Kural says those who fear disgrace will not begin unclear undertakings; Farid likewise steers clear of deeds that lead only to shame.
464.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 59) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
464._accuracy_note: A good fit on shame as a reason for restraint; Farid's shame is before God's court rather than before people, and he does not discuss uncertainty of outcome.

465.quote_or_event: After Guru Arjan's execution, Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, bore two swords for temporal and spiritual authority, trained in arms, built up a Sikh army, fortified his towns and in 1609 built the Akal Takht at Amritsar, recognizing that a clash with Mughal power was coming. Britannica records that his Sikhs later defeated Shah Jahan's armies four times.
465.explanation: Guru Hargobind did not rush into conflict after his father's martyrdom. He first prepared, militarily and institutionally, for a confrontation he saw coming.
465.tie_back: The Kural warns that rising against foes without full preparation only strengthens them; Guru Hargobind's long preparation before facing Mughal forces shows the opposite course.
465._accuracy_note: A historical example rather than a teaching; it fits the call for preparation, but the Kural's specific point (a rash attack strengthens the enemy) has no direct Sikh counterpart.

466.quote_or_event: “You have not done what you should have done; you are entangled in the web of greed. Nanak, your time is past and gone; why are you crying now, you blind fool?”
466.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur rebukes the person who, caught up in greed, leaves undone what ought to have been done, until the time for it has gone.
466.tie_back: The Kural says one is ruined as much by failing to do what ought to be done as by doing what ought not; Guru Tegh Bahadur lays out the ruin of omission.
466.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1428, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 36), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
466._accuracy_note: Strong on the sin of omission; the other half of the Kural (doing what ought not be done) is only implied, and the duty meant is remembering God.

467.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. When you place your feet on this Path, give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
467.explanation: Guru Nanak asks that the full cost be accepted before the first step on the path of love; once the step is taken, there is no holding back.
467.tie_back: The Kural says to think first and then resolve, not to begin and think afterwards; Guru Nanak asks the seeker to settle the price before setting foot on the path, then give without hesitation.
467.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
467._accuracy_note: Matches the order of resolve first and no second thoughts afterwards; it concerns total devotion rather than practical deliberation over an undertaking.

468.quote_or_event: “Hundreds of thousands of clever tricks, but not even one of them will go along with you in the end. … O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will.”
468.explanation: In the first pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says that endless cleverness achieves nothing; only walking in the way of God's will (hukam) succeeds.
468.tie_back: The Kural says effort spent in the wrong way fails whatever help it has; Guru Nanak says countless clever efforts fail unless they follow the right way.
468.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
468._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that effort off the right path is wasted; Gurbani's right way is hukam, not practical method, and the Kural's image of many supporters is absent.

469.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained. Wisdom does not come by reading textbooks; wisdom inspires us to give in charity.”
469.explanation: In Raag Saarang Guru Nanak says that true giving is guided by wisdom, the same discernment that leads to serving God and earning honour.
469.tie_back: The Kural says even doing good can fail without understanding those one deals with; Guru Nanak makes wisdom the guide of charity.
469.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
469._accuracy_note: Reasonable: both want benevolence guided by discernment, but Guru Nanak does not address knowing the particular nature of each recipient.

470.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
470.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak puts truthful conduct above even the knowledge of truth, so that how one lives is the final test.
470.tie_back: The Kural asks for conduct that will not earn the world's scorn; Guru Nanak likewise makes conduct the test, though he measures it by truth rather than by public approval.
470.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
470._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani judges conduct by truth before God, elsewhere tells the devotee to disregard public opinion (Ang 1412), and rejects duty fixed by social station.
